extracted.intended_audience: DHS rulemakers, federal regulators, state attorneys general, and legal advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the DHS Proposed Rule on public charge inadmissibility for legality, administrative reasoned-ness, clarity, and anticipated impacts—particularly on households, bonds, data sharing, and State budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with historical understanding of 'public charge'
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS’s asserted interpretation of the statute is inconsistent with the historical understanding of 'public charge' that Congress has adopted, as repeatedly affirmed by courts of appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule must not expand 'public charge' in a way that affords immigration officers boundless, unregulated discretion; it should be consistent with longstanding congressional intent and judicial precedent (cited cases: New York v. DHS, Cook Cnty. v. Wolf, City & Cnty. of San Francisco v. USCIS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear standard for household benefit use
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule provides no standard as to how benefit use by household members will be treated and instead estimates household-level decisions without explaining whether or how officers will treat non-applicant household members’ use of benefits (including U.S. citizen members).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency must explain whether and how immigration officers will weigh benefits used by household members, provide guardrails to prevent treating household benefit use as presumptively indicative of future dependence, and clarify treatment of benefits accessed by eligible U.S. citizen family members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not delete regulatory definitions without replacements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule removes regulatory definitions and exemptions (e.g., 'public cash assistance for income maintenance,' 'receipt (of public benefits),' and 'long-term institutionalization at government expense') without supplying replacements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If definitions are rescinded, DHS must supply alternative definitions or standards so officers and affected parties can predict enforcement; removing terms that previously limited agency action creates unacceptable uncertainty and arbitrary outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid delegating core policy details to future internal guidance exempt from public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS indicates guidance and training will come 'in the future' as 'policy and interpretive tools,' suggesting issuance without public input or procedural safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core enforcement standards should be in the rule; reliance on future internal guidance (which may be exempt from notice-and-comment under 5 U.S.C. 553) is inadequate. DHS must provide publicly accountable standards now rather than leave them to opaque internal guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the policy that will replace the 2022 Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule represents a significant change without reasoned analysis of what new policy will replace the 2022 Rule; DHS states only that the rescission will 'pave the way' for future policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS must articulate the substantive policy that will apply after rescission, how it differs from the 2019 Rule and the 1999 guidance, and how it will be implemented so States and the public can meaningfully evaluate impacts and comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain 'governing caselaw' relied upon
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS says officers will make determinations consistent with the INA, PRWORA, and 'governing caselaw' but does not identify the caselaw it intends to rely upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule should cite and explain the controlling precedent it views as governing and must not signal an intent to 'depart from—or to selectively invoke—longstanding unbroken judicial precedent' without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond breach standard must be tied to meaningful dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule would make receipt of 'any means-tested benefit' by an applicant noncitizen, without regard to duration, severity, or causation, constitute a breach of a public charge bond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bond cancelation/breach should not be triggered by single, de minimis, or unrelated short-term benefits; the agency must retain a showing of ongoing primary dependence or similar standard and allow mitigating factors and procedural protections before treating benefit receipt as breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain 'dependent on the government for subsistence' focus rather than de minimis enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the 1999 Guidance and the 2022 Rule advised that receipt of public benefits was relevant only where it indicated ongoing primary dependence; the Proposed Rule discards that standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS should preserve the requirement that benefits indicate sustained dependence on government subsistence rather than treating any means-tested use as dispositive or automatically adverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent penalizing immigrants for benefits they did not request or control
rubrics_metrics.description: Immigration officers would be permitted under the Proposed Rule to penalize immigrants for benefits they did not request, did not control, and/or that were legally accessed by U.S. citizen children or other exempt family members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The adjudicatory framework should make clear that benefits lawfully accessed by other household members, or benefits accessed without the applicant's request/control, shall not be treated as evidence of the applicant's likelihood of becoming a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and quantify chilling effects on benefits usage and public health
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule acknowledges disenrollment and 'chilling effects' (e.g., up to 35% in key programs) but treats foregone participation as fiscal savings rather than harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS must analyze how fear, misinformation, and confusion will reduce participation in Medicaid, SNAP, TANF, CHIP, WIC, and other programs; it should not treat decreased enrollment resulting from chilling as an unquestioned fiscal benefit and must quantify public health and community impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze fiscal and administrative impacts on States, including shifted costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule's projected reductions in transfer payments are better understood as lost federal revenue for states and shifted costs (uncompensated emergency care, food banks, local programs) that DHS did not meaningfully analyze.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS must quantify state-level budget impacts, projection of reductions in federal/state transfers, likely increases in uncompensated care and emergency assistance costs, and the net fiscal effect on states and localities, not just 'transfer payment' reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify regulatory familiarization, IT, training, and systems costs for agencies and providers
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS acknowledges 'regulatory familiarization,' staff training, and IT changes but offers no quantitative estimate and treats these burdens as minor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS should provide concrete estimates (drawing on the 2019 Rule implementation experience) for systems reprogramming, vendor changes, retraining eligibility workers, increased transactions costs for providers and community organizations, and other compliance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and analyze reliance interests formed under prior rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule concedes the public may be relying on aspects of the 2022 Final Rule but does not identify or analyze those interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When changing agency policy, DHS must identify reliance interests engendered by prior frameworks, analyze how they arose, and consider alternatives; failure to do so risks arbitrary and capricious decision-making under APA precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary and capricious rulemaking; provide reasoned explanation for departures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule eliminates definitions and replaces them with discretionary enforcement without reasoned analysis or explanation of why prior lists/factors are inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS must engage with the reasons it previously adopted particular factors and standards (e.g., the 2019 finite factor list), explain why it is departing from them, and provide reasoned decision-making supported by record evidence to satisfy APA standards (see Encino Motorcars and other cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify scope and limits of any proposed data sharing and protect privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule contains a vague reference to 'data sharing' that will chill benefits use and may violate federal privacy statutes (Social Security Act, HIPAA, 42 U.S.C. § 290dd-2/42 C.F.R. pt. 2, Privacy Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS must specify what data it intends to collect/share, explain how the data will be used, and ensure any programmatic data sharing complies with statutory privacy protections; it should evaluate chilling effects from data sharing and propose safeguards or limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide procedural protections and notice for individuals facing bond breach or adverse findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule offers no identified procedural protection for individuals subject to bond breach or the proposed 'single benefit use = breach' approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS should identify due-process and procedural safeguards (notice, opportunity to rebut, mitigation, individualized assessment) before imposing bond breach or other severe enforcement consequences tied to benefit use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for heterogeneity across States to avoid unequal treatment based on state program structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Because states differ in how they structure, fund, and classify public benefit programs, households with identical income, family size, and immigration status may be treated differently for bond or public-charge purposes depending solely on their state of residence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS must consider state program variation, avoid rules that make enforcement depend on state-specific program design, and provide uniform standards or adjust analyses to prevent arbitrary geographic disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat reduced participation by eligible persons as a regulatory benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS treats reductions in enrollment due to fear or misinformation as a mere 'reduction in transfer payments' (an $8.97 billion annual 'saving'), rather than as social or fiscal harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rulemaking must distinguish between direct eligibility changes and enrollment declines caused by chilling; DHS should not count fear-driven disenrollment as a regulatory benefit and must account for social costs and shifted burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide actionable, public-facing guidance on how officers will apply the INA totality-of-the-circumstances test
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS asserts officers will make case-by-case determinations under the INA totality-of-the-circumstances test and PRWORA without explaining how officers will weigh factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If DHS relies on a 'totality' approach it should explain factor weighting, provide examples, and issue transparent, publicly accessible instructions so affected parties and States can anticipate outcomes and comment meaningfully.
